issues.legal_issue: The statutory stay on proceedings against a sick industrial company applies to the proceedings specified by law when they can obstruct the formulation or implementation of its rehabilitation scheme, even if the relevant dues were not included in the scheme.
material_facts: The company had been declared sick and a rehabilitation scheme was being considered and implemented.
The company’s land and the proceeds from its sale were important to the proposed revival.
The court considered whether proceedings and recoveries concerning a sick company were protected only when the relevant dues had been included in its rehabilitation scheme.
issues.conclusion: The stay is not confined to dues included in a sanctioned scheme. It applies where proceedings fall within the statutory categories and have the potential to interfere with formulation, consideration, finalization or implementation of the scheme; they may proceed with the consent of the competent rehabilitation authority.
issues.legal_principle: The court construed Section 22(1) of the Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985 broadly but not without limits: the proceedings must fall within the categories specified there and affect the rehabilitation scheme. It reconciled Shree Vallabh Glass Works Ltd. v. Shree Vallabh Glass Works Ltd., Corromandal Pharmaceuticals, Jay Engineering Works Ltd. v. Industry Facilitation Council, and Shree Sajjan Mills Ltd. v. Municipal Corporation, Ratlam by reference to their facts. It also relied on Maharashtra Tubes Ltd. v. State Industrial and Investment Corporation of Maharashtra, Tata Davy Ltd. v. State of Orissa, and Morgan Securities and Credit Pvt. Ltd. in describing the breadth of the protection.

rule.if: sick_company_rehabilitation_proceeding and (specified_asset_recovery_proceeding or money_recovery_suit) and (proceeding_can_obstruct_scheme or recovery_can_divert_company_assets)

predicates.sick_company_rehabilitation_proceeding: A proceeding concerns an industrial company whose sickness is under inquiry or whose rehabilitation scheme is being prepared, considered or implemented.
predicates.specified_asset_recovery_proceeding: A party seeks winding up, execution, distress, a receiver, or another proceeding of the same kind against the company or its property.
predicates.money_recovery_suit: A party brings a suit to recover money or enforce security or a guarantee against the company.
predicates.proceeding_can_obstruct_scheme: The proceeding is capable of interfering with formulation, consideration, finalization or implementation of the company’s rehabilitation scheme.
predicates.recovery_can_divert_company_assets: The recovery could remove or divert company assets needed for rehabilitation.

issues.definition: When a specified recovery proceeding or money-recovery suit in a sick-company rehabilitation proceeding can obstruct the scheme or divert needed assets, the competent authority’s consent is required before it proceeds.

issues.legal_issue: During the statutory rehabilitation process, the rehabilitation authority may suspend or adapt pre-existing contracts and related rights or liabilities when necessary for implementing the scheme.
material_facts: The land-sale memorandum of understanding and principal agreement were made before the company presented its reference to the rehabilitation authority.
A supplementary agreement was made while the rehabilitation scheme was pending, and another was made after the authority had acted on the scheme.
The company’s land and the expected sale proceeds were considered in the restructuring and were material to the revival scheme.
The authority directed that disposal of assets required its prior approval and sought details concerning the land and the proposed sale.
issues.conclusion: The authority’s powers under Section 22(3) extended to the pre-existing sale arrangements and permitted it to suspend or adapt their operation for the limited purpose of implementing the rehabilitation scheme, subject to the statutory limits.
issues.legal_principle: Section 22(3) of the Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985 authorizes suspension of the operation of contracts, assurances of property, agreements and other instruments, and permits rights, privileges, obligations and liabilities under them to be suspended or enforced with adaptations specified by the authority. Section 22(4) gives such a declaration overriding effect and provides for revival of suspended rights and proceedings when it ceases; the proviso to Section 22(3) limits its duration. Sections 22, 22A and 32 must be read together. The court relied on the statutory scheme and the reasoning in Jay Engineering Works Ltd. and Morgan Securities and Credit Pvt. Ltd.

predicates.sick_company_rehabilitation_proceeding: A rehabilitation inquiry or scheme concerning a sick industrial company is pending or being implemented.
predicates.pre_existing_company_instrument: The company was a party to, or subject to, the contract or other instrument before the relevant authority order.
predicates.instrument_affects_scheme_implementation: The contract or instrument concerns assets or obligations material to implementing the company’s rehabilitation scheme.

issues.definition: If a pre-existing instrument of a sick company affects implementation of its rehabilitation scheme, the authority may suspend or adapt that instrument for the scheme’s implementation.

issues.legal_issue: The special rehabilitation law governing sick industrial companies prevails over general property-transfer law where their operation conflicts in relation to rehabilitation measures.
material_facts: The purchaser relied on property-transfer rules concerning sale agreements and possession to argue that the rehabilitation authority could not restrict completion of the land transfer.
The land and sale proceeds were part of the company’s rehabilitation arrangements.
The court compared the special law governing sick industrial companies with the general law governing transfers of immovable property.
issues.conclusion: The special rehabilitation law prevails over the general property-transfer law in the event of conflict, and property-transfer protections do not prevent the rehabilitation authority from exercising its statutory powers.
issues.legal_principle: The court treated the Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985 as a special, self-contained law with an overriding effect, including under Sections 22 and 32, and treated the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 as general law. It relied on the special-law principle and on Tata Motors Ltd., Jay Engineering Works Ltd., Tata Davy Ltd., and NGEF Ltd. v. Chandra Developers (P) Ltd.

predicates.sick_company_rehabilitation_proceeding: A rehabilitation proceeding concerns an industrial company declared sick under the applicable rehabilitation framework.
predicates.property_transfer_claim_conflicts_with_r: A party invokes a general property-transfer right in a way that would prevent or restrict a measure within the rehabilitation authority’s statutory control.

issues.definition: Where a property-transfer claim conflicts with statutory control in a sick-company rehabilitation proceeding, the special rehabilitation control prevails.

issues.legal_issue: A contract for sale of immovable property does not itself transfer ownership or create an interest or charge in the property.
material_facts: The parties had made a memorandum of understanding and agreements for the sale of the company’s land.
The purchaser relied on those agreements to claim an interest in the land, although the court was not deciding the merits or enforceability of the parties’ contractual rights.
issues.conclusion: An agreement to sell does not itself create title, an interest or a charge in the immovable property.
issues.legal_principle: Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 distinguishes a sale from a contract for sale and states that a contract for sale does not, of itself, create any interest in or charge on the property. The court relied on Rambaran Prosad v. Ram Mohit Hazra and reiterated the position stated in State of U.P. v. District Judge, Dharma Naika v. Rama Naika, and Mrs. Saradamani Kandappan v. Rajalakshmi.

predicates.immovable_property_sale_dispute: The dispute concerns an asserted transfer of immovable property by sale.
predicates.only_contract_for_sale_without_completed: The claimant relies on a contract to sell but no completed conveyance of ownership has occurred.

issues.definition: A claimant relying only on a contract to sell, without a completed conveyance, does not obtain title through that contract.

issues.legal_issue: Possession taken in part performance gives a limited protection against the transferor but does not confer ownership or defeat the rehabilitation authority’s statutory control.
material_facts: The purchaser claimed that possession had been delivered under a supplementary agreement.
The purchaser relied on part performance to resist restrictions on completion of the transfer.
The land was a material company asset considered in the rehabilitation scheme.
issues.conclusion: Even if possession in part performance is accepted, it does not create title; the resulting protection is limited and does not displace the overriding rehabilitation law.
issues.legal_principle: Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 recognizes a limited right arising from part performance, but does not transfer ownership. State of U.P. v. District Judge explains that the protection operates as a shield against the transferor and does not alter the transferor’s ownership before a lawful conveyance. The special rehabilitation law prevails over the general property-transfer law where they conflict.

predicates.immovable_property_sale_dispute: The dispute concerns rights claimed under an agreement to transfer immovable property.
predicates.possession_taken_in_part_performance: The proposed transferee has taken possession in performance of the agreement.
predicates.no_completed_conveyance: Ownership has not been transferred by a completed conveyance.
predicates.rehabilitation_control: A rehabilitation authority is exercising statutory control over the property or transaction as part of a sick company’s scheme.

issues.definition: Possession taken in part performance without a completed conveyance does not give title and does not override rehabilitation control.

issues.legal_issue: The rehabilitation authority may restrict completion of a land sale when the land is a material asset of the sick company and the transaction is connected with its rehabilitation scheme.
material_facts: The company’s principal land was treated as a major asset and the expected sale proceeds were part of its restructuring and revival arrangements.
The rehabilitation authority considered the sale, sought details about the land and its valuation, and required prior approval for disposal of assets.
A later supplementary agreement providing for possession and accelerated payments was made after the authority had acted on the rehabilitation scheme and without its prior approval.
The appellate rehabilitation body allowed the sale to proceed without restriction, but the High Court restored the authority’s restrictions.
issues.conclusion: The authority had jurisdiction to restrict transfer of the land pending the scheme, and the High Court correctly restored its order; the appeals were dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 22(1), 22(3), 22A and 32 of the Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985 give the rehabilitation authority wide powers to protect scheme formulation and implementation, including powers over company assets and relevant agreements. Section 22A addresses restraint on disposal of assets during preparation or consideration of a scheme, while Section 22 has a wider reach through the scheme’s consideration and implementation. The court applied its construction of these provisions and the principle that rehabilitation schemes should remain free from obstruction.

rule.if: sick_company_rehabilitation_proceeding and land_is_material_rehabilitation_asset and sale_is_connected_to_scheme and proposed_transfer_lacks_authority_approval

predicates.sick_company_rehabilitation_proceeding: A rehabilitation proceeding is pending or the scheme for a sick industrial company is being implemented.
predicates.land_is_material_rehabilitation_asset: The land is a significant asset needed or relied upon in the company’s rehabilitation.
predicates.sale_is_connected_to_scheme: The proposed sale or its proceeds form part of, or materially affect, the rehabilitation arrangements.
predicates.proposed_transfer_lacks_authority_approv: The proposed transfer or a material later arrangement concerning it has not received the authority’s required approval.

issues.definition: When a sale concerns land material to a sick company’s rehabilitation scheme and the required approval has not been obtained, the authority may restrict the transfer while the scheme is pending.
